holding: This and connected appeals are meritless and same are, hereby, dismissed. No order as to the costs. (Asim Hafeez) Judge

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing 27.10.2026 For the appellant Mr. Dost Muhammad Kahoot, Advocate. For the Respondent Ch. Muhammad Naseer Gujjar, Advocate. ASIM HAFEEZ, J. This and connected appeals, bearing R.F.A Nos. 51948/2025 and 51714/2025, converge on a lone controversial question; that whether parties owe each other any amount of money and is cheque subject matter of instant appeal is enforceable – though parties have instituted two separate suits and same were decided through separate judgments. Appellant invoked summary jurisdiction procedure in terms of Order XXXVII of Civil Procedure Code 1908 and claimed recovery on the basis of cheque / negotiable instrument. And conversely, respondent approached Civil Court and sought reliefs comprising of declaration-cum-rendition of accounts, recovery of monetary damages and ineffectiveness of the cheque in question – latter suit was transferred for adjudication to the Additional District Judge Lahore under the orders of this Court; where the former suit was pending and leave to defend was granted. Upon adjudication, the Court of first instance dismissed the claim of recovery, based on cheque, after recording of evidence, and simultaneously, suit for declaration-cum- rendition was partly decreed, to the extent of recovery of cheque, rendering it ineffective. Hence, these Appeals.

Primary argument of appellant’s counsel is that witnesses of delivery of cheque were produced, who had proved the factum of delivery and consequent acknowledgement of liability but court failed to appreciate the evidence. It is further argued that liability against respondent, in lieu of the commercial transactions, was proved through producing ledger of accounts, which is Exh.P-9, and it contained details of transactions effected and payable balance, which was secured through tendering of cheque, which bounced.

Conversely, learned counsel for respondent submits that cheque was not meant for presentation but it was a security cheque and unless condition of proving the liability was fulfilled no claim could be raised. Submits that feed supplied were sub-standard and no amount was payable. Adds that Exh.P-9 was the copy prepared for the claim and unless original register / books of supply and payments was produced no decree could be granted. And no direct and credible evidence was produced to prove any payable liability.

This is one of those unusual cases where respondent, the drawer of cheque, was not required to bring an independent and convincing evidence to prove that delivery of cheque was conditional, which in commercial parlance is called a security cheque. Instrument contained an indorsement on the back of the cheque; expressed as “security cheque”. An obvious fact was reiterated by PW-5, an officer of the Bank, who appeared and affirmed that cheque was qualified by the condition, ‘security cheque’. This indorsement has two-fold significance. Firstly, drawee’s right to enforce cheque was subjected to a condition and unless condition was fulfilled there is no question of presenting it for encashment. Secondly, conditionality attached removes the statutory presumption otherwise claimable under section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881. What is the nature and effect of the condition – qualifying instrument as security cheque. In wake of the commercial relations between the parties – supply-cum-sale and purchase of feed – it is evident that security cheque was delivered conditionally with an understanding that unless liability of the respondent is reconciled, mutually or otherwise, no enforceability thereof could be claimed. In simple words, liability under the principal contract has to be established. This constitutes an encumbrance over drawee’s right to enforce alleged obligation under the cheque. On facts, learned counsel for appellant relies on Exh.P-9, claimed as a ledger. Whether Exh.P-9 meet tests of admissibility, credibility and probability of proving alleged claim – condition of security cheque. Exh.P-9 is a private document, which is a copy or reflection of sale/purchase register or books of accounts, and is treated as a secondary document in terms of Article 74 of Qanun-e-Shahadat Order 1984. Apparently, no permission was sought to produce secondary evidence, therefore, Exh.P-9 is not legally receivable in evidence and same is inadmissible. Exh.P-9 fails test of credibility. Reading of Exh.P-9 manifest it was ledger of an entity, namely, M.A Farm. When asked, learned counsel for appellant referred to the agreement, containing bargain between appellant and respondent – which was between appellant and in the name of respondent and cheque was issued against personal account of the respondent. How ledger of M.A Farm could be treated and construed as proof of liability of respondent; learned counsel read clause (12) of the agreement of supply of feeds and pleaded that respondent is a sole proprietor of M.A Farm. I read clause 12 of the agreement whose scope is different, which treated M.A. Farm as an entity, having assets. And said clause otherwise envisages encumbering assets of M.A Farm. This was not the case of the appellant that M.A Farm was the proprietorship concern and respondent was its sole proprietor. PW-4, who presented Exh.P-9, admitted that underlying record of said exhibit was not available with him and there were no signatures of respondent. PW-4 did not say that respondent was proprietor of M.A Farm. PW-4 stated that respondent purchased feed of Rs.8,371,000/- and paid Rs.4,421,000 and Rs.3,950,000/- was payable, which was allegedly secured through cheque. This outstanding balance has to be proved by producing purchase and supply orders and details of payments received and overdue – this exercise is essential when cheque contained indorsement of a security cheque. Be that as it may, even if argument is considered plausible for sake of adjudication, still no liability could be established on the basis of Exh.P-9, which contained details of purchase orders but no such purchase orders were not produced, in respect whereof amounts were claimed due. This denudes Exh.P-9 of any credibility. And with respect to probability of existence of proving of claim, it is clear that upon perusal of unconvincing evidence, even if considered to be legally receivable, probability of absence of liability is more obvious. Mere production of witnesses to claim that cheque was issued was not sufficient but fulfilment of condition attached must be proved to seek enforcement of cheque.

Now the question arises that whether alleged defence that cheque was a security cheque, therefore, mere delivery thereof does not make it per se enforceable. Upon perusal of the provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, it appears that such defence has statutory footing and section 46 thereof deals with the conditionally attached by way of indorsement of a security cheque. It is appropriate to reproduce the text of section 46, which reads as; “46. Delivery. The making, acceptance or indorsement of a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque is completed by delivery, actual or constructive. As between parties standing in immediate relation, delivery to be effectual must be made by the party making, accepting or indorsing the instrument or by a person authorized by him in that behalf. As between such parties and any holder of the instrument other than a holder in due course, it may be shown that the instrument was delivered conditionally or for a special purpose only, and not for the purpose of transferring absolutely the property therein. A Promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to bearer is negotiable by the delivery thereof. A promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to order is negotiable by the holder by indorsement and delivery thereof”.

Paragraph second of section 46 is aptly attracted. Indorsement on the cheque implies delivery with a condition or for a special purpose, which dismisses claim of per se enforcement of the cheque – condition attached must be fulfilled, that is proof of liabilities under principal contract, and unless done, no claim could be raised for recovery under said instrument. And benchmark of proof of proving liability, under a cheque, is higher when presumption under section 118 of Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 is not available in context of condition attached. I find no illegality qua dismissal of claim of the appellant.

Learned counsel for the respondent, appellant in RFA No. 51948 of 2025 also failed to show any illegality in the judgment, whereby his claim of damages was dismissed – mere claim of damages is not enough but underlying basis thereof has to be proved but respondent, appellant of RFA No.51948/2025, failed to discharge burden.

This and connected appeals are meritless and same are, hereby, dismissed. No order as to the costs. (Asim Hafeez) Judge Announced in open Court on this 06th day of November, 2026. (Asim Hafeez) Judge Approved for reporting. Judge *M. Nadeem/*
